title: A vector field and its flow lines: which way does the flow go?
summary: Short arrows give the local direction and size of a field at grid points; streamlines show where the flow goes globally. Together they show sources, sinks, circulation and closed orbits.

media.alt: A square plot with teal arrows on a coarse grid and blue streamlines spiralling outward from a pink dot at the origin and inward from outside onto a thick orange circle, which is marked as a stable limit cycle.
media.caption: Reference render of class F2.4 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: Which way does the flow go?
read_the_figure.axes: x and y in the plane, equal scale, -1.8 to 1.8. Teal arrows: the field at an 11 by 11 grid; their length is speed times 0.2 data units (the key above the plot). Blue lines: streamlines, tangent to the field everywhere. Amber circle: the limit cycle, rose dot: the unstable focus.
look_at: Which way do the streamlines rotate and what happens at r = 1?
What do streamlines do far inside and far outside the circle: spiral away or toward it?
How long are the arrows near the circle compared with outside? Use the key.
Where would a particle placed near the origin end up?
as_drawn: The field is V = (-y + x(1 - r^2), x + y(1 - r^2)) with r^2 = x^2 + y^2. It rotates counter-clockwise at unit angular speed and pushes outward inside r = 1 and inward outside.
The arrow key says 'speed 1.0 = arrow length 0.2 (data units)'. On the circle the speed is r = 1, so those arrows are 0.2 long.
Arrows lie on top of streamlines; near the edges the picture is crowded, and the legend covers some streamlines at top left.
read_the_figure.proves: The qualitative global structure of this field: a repelling point at the origin and an attracting closed orbit at r = 1. It does not prove that nothing else, such as a small closed orbit hidden between streamlines, is present.
if_wrong: Arrows normalised to equal length without a note: size information is lost.
Arrow scale not given: speeds cannot be read.
Streamlines seeded too sparsely: structure between lines is missed.

terms.meaning: A rule that attaches a vector (direction and size) to every point.
A curve everywhere tangent to the field at one instant. For a steady field it is also the path of a particle.
An isolated closed orbit that nearby paths approach (stable) or leave (unstable).
An equilibrium that nearby paths spiral around.
A reference arrow with a stated value that fixes the arrow scale.

remember: Streamlines never cross, except at zero-field points.
Arrow length is speed times a stated factor; give the key.
Arrows show local value, streamlines show global topology; use both.
Streamlines are particle paths only for steady fields.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Each teal arrow has a position (where the field is sampled), a direction (the vector's direction) and a length (its size, with a scale given by the key). Each blue line has a position and an arrowhead for direction only. The thick amber line and the rose dot are annotations from analysis, not data.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A field is a function with two outputs at every point, so it cannot be a curve. Arrows give the value at sampled points; streamlines connect the arrows into global paths, which is what a person wants to know: where does a particle go. The combination turns local information into topology: circling, repelling, attracting.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Arrow length is easy to misread when arrows are scaled; normalised arrows hide speed. A coarse grid or sparse seeding hides small features. A steady-field streamline is not a path in an unsteady field. Overplotting arrows and streamlines clutters the picture where the field is strong.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: The arrow-scale key lets the reader convert length to speed. Streamlines carry the global story the arrows cannot. Both are required because each fails alone: arrows give magnitude but no topology; streamlines give topology but no magnitude.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Colour the streamlines by speed so a single layer shows both. A line-integral convolution shows texture over the whole plane. For nullclines and fixed points use a phase portrait (F4.7). For an unsteady field use pathlines or streaklines. For a strictly rotational check, plot the divergence and curl maps.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Colour the streamlines by speed, delete the quiver layer, and add a small inset with r(t) for two starting points, one inside and one outside the circle.

steps.title: Polar form of the field
steps.note: Writing x = r cos(theta), y = r sin(theta) separates the field: the angular part is a constant rotation, the radial part has equilibria at r = 0 and r = 1.

steps.title: Stability of the circle
steps.note: The slope of the radial speed is -2 at r = 1 (stable) and +1 at the origin (unstable). Numerically, starts at r = 0.1 and r = 2 both reach r = 1.00001 at t = 30.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) which way is the circulation? (2) What is the speed on the circle and how long is the arrow? (3) What does a particle near the origin do?

solution.text: Counter-clockwise: the streamlines and arrows turn left around the origin.
On r = 1 the radial speed is zero and the angular speed is 1, so |v| = r = 1 and the arrow has length 0.2 by the key.
It spirals outward, because the origin is an unstable focus (radial rate r(1 - r^2) is positive for r < 1), and approaches the circle.

worked.answer: Counter-clockwise flow; unit speed on the circle; paths spiral out from the origin onto the limit cycle r = 1.

analyze.q: Both families of streamlines approach the circle. How can you tell a stable limit cycle from an unstable one by looking at the arrowheads?
analyze.hint: Which way do neighbouring lines point?

analyze.q: Where are the arrows longest and why?
analyze.hint: Speed is r times the radial factor.

analyze.q: What would normalised arrows (all the same length) hide in this field?

evaluate.q: A fluid simulation's streamline picture looks smooth but the arrows near a wall look wrong. Which layer do you trust and what do you check?

create: Redraw with streamlines coloured by speed and a quiver key in physical units.
Plot a time series r(t) for three initial radii to show convergence to 1.

checks.q: What is the difference between a streamline and a pathline?
checks.answer: A streamline is tangent to the field at one instant; a pathline is the track of one particle through time. They agree only for steady fields.

checks.q: The key says speed 1.0 is an arrow of 0.2 units. How long is an arrow where speed is 3?
Streamlines look like closed loops, but the field has a small drift. Could the picture mislead?
checks.answer: Yes: a slow outward or inward spiral can look like a closed orbit over the plotted range. Check the radial rate along an orbit.
